title: Hormuz Crisis Costs Fossil Fuel Importers $330 Billion as India Pays $22 Billion Extra
excerpt: A new CREA analysis finds the six-month energy price shock is the largest since the 1990 Gulf War, with low-income countries bearing a disproportionate burden.
body:
• Global fossil fuel import bills surged by $330 billion in six months since the Hormuz crisis began, the largest sustained oil price shock since the 1990 Gulf War, according to CREA
  • India paid an extra $22 billion for fossil fuel imports from March to August 2026 — the third-highest additional cost after the EU ($78 billion) and China ($35 billion)
  • Asian LNG prices averaged 75% above pre-war expectations, European LNG 60% above, diesel 59% above, and crude oil 35% above during the period
  • Clean power generation added since 2020 saved importing countries an estimated $36 billion in avoided fossil fuel costs during the crisis

The Strait of Hormuz crisis has cost fossil fuel importers worldwide more than $330 billion in additional costs over its first six months, making it the largest sustained oil and gas price shock since Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait in 1990, according to a new analysis by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

The staggering figure, covering the period from March to August 2026, represents approximately $55 billion in extra costs per month for countries that depend on seaborne crude oil, refined products, and LNG imports.

India Among the Hardest Hit

In absolute terms, the European Union bore the highest additional cost at $78 billion, followed by China at $35 billion and India at $22 billion. But the burden has fallen disproportionately on poorer nations: the typical low- or middle-income country paid roughly twice as much relative to GDP as the typical high-income country, the CREA report found.

For India, which imports approximately 88% of the crude oil it consumes daily, the $22 billion hit compounds an already-challenging fiscal picture. About 40% of India's crude oil imports, 60% of its LNG imports, and 90% of its LPG imports normally transit through the Strait of Hormuz. With Russia filling part of the gap — Indian purchases of Russian crude hit a record high in June, up 34% month-on-month — the import bill has still ballooned as global benchmark prices remain elevated.

Price Shocks Across Every Fuel

The scale of the price dislocation is remarkable across every major fuel category. Asian LNG prices averaged 75% above what pre-war futures markets had implied, European LNG prices 60% above, diesel and gas oil 59% above, and crude oil 35% above pre-conflict expectations.

The diesel price increase alone has had cascading effects. CREA found that 134 of the 170 countries in its analysis paid more for diesel than pre-war futures had predicted — making it the most widely felt impact of the crisis, given diesel's role in transportation, agriculture, and industrial production.

"The best way to protect against high oil prices is to get off the black stuff as quickly as possible. The energy transition is an investment."

— Luke Wickenden, Energy Analyst, CREA

Clean Energy as a Shield

One notable finding from the CREA analysis: clean power generation capacity added worldwide since 2020 saved importing countries an estimated $36 billion in avoided coal, gas, and oil purchases during the first five months of the crisis. The report noted that the monthly cost of the crisis to fossil fuel importers equaled total global investment in renewable power in 2025.

The data provides a concrete economic argument for accelerating the energy transition — not as a climate policy alone, but as a hedge against the kind of supply shock the Hormuz crisis represents.

Inflation Pressure Builds

The energy price surge is feeding through to broader inflation. U.S. consumer prices rose 3.4% in July year-over-year, driven partly by a 14.7% increase in energy costs and a 24.6% jump in gasoline prices. Euro-zone inflation accelerated to 2.9%, led by a 10% rise in energy costs. Japan's producer price index climbed 7.2% in July.

With more than 20 refineries across the Gulf damaged during the conflict and repair timelines stretching years, energy analysts warn the supply squeeze may persist well beyond any diplomatic resolution. The Reserve Bank of India is widely expected to hold its key interest rate at 5.25% in 2026, but a sustained energy-driven inflation spike could force a reassessment.
